title: The Conference of the Birds
text:
In this Persian poem by Farid ud-Din Attar, the birds of the world gathered because they had no king. The hoopoe, the wisest among them, told them they did have one, the Simurgh, who lived far away beyond the mountains of Qaf. The journey to reach him was long and terrible, but they should go.

At first the birds were eager, and then each found an excuse. The nightingale could not leave its love for the rose. The parrot wanted immortality rather than a king. The peacock longed for paradise, the duck could not leave the water, the hawk was content serving earthly kings, and so on. The hoopoe answered each one with a story.

At last a great flock set out. They had to cross seven valleys: of the quest, of love, of understanding, of detachment, of unity, of bewilderment, and of poverty and annihilation. Many birds died or turned back along the way.

Only thirty birds finally reached the Simurgh's court. When the veil was lifted, they looked upon the Simurgh, and in it they saw themselves. In Persian, si murgh means thirty birds. What they had traveled so far to find was what they had become together.
lesson: A group sometimes discovers that the strength it was looking for outside was in its own members all along, but only after they have gone through the hard road together.
people: The hoopoe, the birds, the Simurgh
source: Farid ud-Din Attar, The Conference of the Birds (Mantiq al-Tayr)
